subject: 🐛 Anthropic's 1,000-agent swarm catches 66/70 bugs in parallel
intro: The coding agent wars just got a hardware upgrade. Anthropic ships 1,000-agent swarms. OpenAI teaches Codex to predict your next message. Both point at the same thing: the bottleneck is no longer the model, it's the interface around it. More agents, less typing. AI tools are quietly absorbing the cognitive overhead of using AI tools. That's a loop worth watching. A new paper reminds us that smarter context trimming often beats throwing more compute at the problem.

news.headline: Anthropic launches Claude managed agents, coordinating up to 1,000 agents per run
news.body: Imagine asking one AI to review a 116,000-line codebase for bugs. It finds maybe 27. Now imagine spinning up 1,000 agents working in parallel on the same job. They find 66 out of 70 bugs , consistently, every single run. That's the gap Claude's new dynamic workflows just opened up. Here's how it works: one lead agent writes a plan, splits the work into phases, and hands tasks off to a swarm of worker agents. They run in parallel, then merge results at the end. You don't manage any of that coordination yourself. What you can now tackle: To turn it on, set multiagent type: multiagent_20261001 in your agent config. Start small, since these workflows burn tokens fast. Kick things off in Claude Code with: /claude-api managed-agents-onboard bug-hunter
bullets: Reviewing hundreds of documents at once
Large-scale bug hunting across massive codebases
Any task too big for a single context window

news.headline: Open-source tool turns one-line descriptions into interactive 3D machine diagrams with Claude
news.body: Docs diagrams are usually dead boxes and arrows. Anatomy fixes that. It's a free Claude Code skill that turns one line of text into a fully interactive, rotatable machine illustration. The clever part: it maps your concept to a physical object . A rate limiter becomes a pin-tumbler lock. A GPU serving many canvases becomes a gantry plotter with 16 arms. The machine's mechanics mirror how your concept actually works. What you get: Install it with one command: npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a claude-code . Then type /anatomy followed by your idea. Add the word "interactive" and it moves. Leave it out and you get a still drawing. Perfect for docs, articles, and landing pages.
bullets: Rotatable isometric SVG figures you can drag, hover, and explore with your keyboard
WebGL shaders for fire, water, and plasma layered inside the drawing
A true 3D mode where parts spin in depth (slow to build, but impressive)
Zero npm dependencies, no API keys needed

news.headline: AirLLM runs Llama 405B on just 8GB of VRAM with no quantization
news.body: No GPU? No problem. AirLLM just made that excuse obsolete. Normally, running a 70-billion-parameter AI model needs around 140GB of VRAM , that's two enterprise A100 GPUs costing tens of thousands of dollars. AirLLM loads one layer at a time into GPU memory, runs the computation, saves the result, then swaps in the next. A 70B model runs on just 4GB of VRAM, at full precision. Think of it like reading a book one page at a time instead of memorizing the whole thing. Here's what you get out of the box: Speed is traded for accessibility , it's slower than full-VRAM inference, but you can now run private, local AI on hardware you already own. Get started with pip install airllm .
bullets: 70B models on 4GB VRAM , 405B on 8GB , no expensive hardware needed
No quantization (model quality stays intact) , optional 4-bit mode for up to 3x speed
Supports Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek on Linux, Windows, and macOS
